newsitem.title: UK: EU grains buckle under increasing surplus pressure.
newsitem.headline: EU grains buckle under increasing surplus pressure.

text.p: Grain prices slithered in most of Europe this week as supply pressures intensified and the European Commission looked keen to force them lower before allowing more exports.
Wheat was hit almost everywhere, except Germany which continued to respond to eastern European orders. But demand was trickling there also and the Hamburg exchange marked its prices down.
Maize held steady across Europe as crop watchers continued to receive mixed signals on harvest progress. Barley remained firm.

The latest forecast of record European crops this year came from the farmers' organisation COPA, which saw the total harvest at 205.1 million tonnes, four million tonnes higher than the figure by the traders' association COCERAL.
But the EU policy makers seemed in no rush to concede a swift export programme while grain prices hovered well above intervention in France and Germany.
"The Commission is expected to announce measures to force down domestic prices, most likely by rejecting or limiting export refunds," said one source close to the EU policy makers.
Traders were edgy before the weekly tender on Thursday, saying a disappointing outcome could send prices lower.
"If we don't get a good result on Thursday, prices will start to fall again and no-one can even guess where the bottom is," said one UK trader.
French wheat slipped further this week with news the French farm ministry had revised up its harvest figure to 34.57 million tonnes from the previous 34.15 million, undermining prices.
Maize was broadly unchanged while scattered rain slowed down the harvest, but traders suspected the firmness would not last.
"Rain is delaying the price drop but it would take only a few days of fine weather for prices to slip," one dealer said.
French maize was already flooding into Spain's northern region of Catalonia, pressuring prices there. But traders saw the market stabilising around 26,000 pesetas.

Maize was mixed elsewhere in Spain. It was offered at 24,600 pesetas in the eastern region of Extremadura which started harvesting early while origin prices in Albacete were between 26,000 and 26,500.
In Britain, wheat lost its toehold under a strong sterling while traders fought to stay competitive against other European suppliers.
"In order to remain competitive we had to lower prices because we have a large surplus," said one trader.
Feed wheat delivered to East Anglia for Oct-Dec dates fetched 102 stg per tonne on Wednesday, down from 105 last week.
But barley held relatively steady on the heels of a large order recently from Saudi Arabia, sought partly from European sources.
German farmers continued to withhold grain in the hope of higher prices next year, shrugging off signs that consumer interest is diminishing.
Italian soft wheat was stable and the Institute for Agriculture Studies (Ismea) forecast prices to remain at current levels for the rest of the season.
"Many market participants were able to buy foreign soft wheat from abroad at the beginning of the crop season when internal supply was still scarce," said Ismea.
In addition, many feed producers were no longer buying soft wheat, awaiting the maize turnout which Ismea forecast at 9.2 milion tonnes, up from 8.5 million last year.
But the forecast was preliminary, not taking account of torrential rains in northern Italy recently which delayed the harvest substantially.
Spanish barley held firm as farmers held back stock until January for fiscal reasons. One trader reckoned barley was some 1,500 pesetas overpriced considering the amount of pent-up supply.
